claims.text: Depositing a thin, conformal Ni interlayer on W particles before Cu infiltration will enhance Cu wettability.
The Ni interlayer will improve W–Cu interfacial bonding.
The Ni interlayer will reduce void formation and phase separation in W–Cu composites.
The Ni-coated composite will preserve mechanical integrity under irradiation better than a conventional vapor-coated W-powder baseline.
W–Cu matrices made by powder consolidation or vapor coating typically contain phase separation and voids that limit thermal transport.
A nanoscale Ni or similar wetting-promoting layer can be deposited on W before Cu filling and sintering.
Low-temperature coating will avoid alteration of the W microstructure.
A sintering temperature below the W melting point can still permit Cu infiltration and W–Cu–Ni interdiffusion.
A continuous Ni interlayer will act as a diffusion bridge at the W–Cu interface.
The Ni interlayer will reduce W–Cu interfacial energy.
Reduced interfacial energy and controlled interdiffusion will create a graded W–Ni–Cu interface.
The graded interface will preserve thermal conductivity and mechanical durability during high-temperature irradiation service.
Relative to sintered vapor-coated W powders, Ni-coated W composites will have a more uniform, less defective interface.
Relative to the named baseline, Ni-coated W composites will have enhanced thermal transport and mechanical stability under irradiation.
Spark-plasma-sintered or mechanically alloyed powder systems can exhibit heterogeneous, multiphase microstructures.
Spark-plasma sintering of vapor-coated W powders or mechanical alloying of elemental W–Cu powders often yields voids and phase separation.
Tungsten melts at approximately 3422 °C.
Irradiation up to a few dpa is representative of fusion-reactor joint service.
Ar+, He+, and D+ ion-beam exposures can simulate the relevant fusion-reactor irradiation conditions for this comparison.
The optimal Ni-layer thickness and its long-term irradiation stability are uncertain.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis characterizes vapor-coated W powders as typically defective and uses them as an inferior baseline, whereas the task context describes vapor-coated W powders as having achieved near-perfect constituent contact. The hypothesis does not reconcile this baseline characterization.
